title.narrative: Nepal Fourth Financial Sector Stability Credit DPC4

description.narrative: The objective of the credit is to support the financial sector medium-term reform program initiated by the Nepalese authorities to reduce the vulnerability of the banking sector and increase its transparency.

This is the fourth operation in a series of Development Policy Credit (DPC) operations with thedevelopment objective of supporting the Government of Nepal's (GoN) financial sector medium-termreform to reduce the vulnerability of the banking sector and increase its transparency. This program document describes the Fourth Financial Sector Stability Development Policy Credit (DPC4) to the GoN, in the amount of SDR 71.1 million (US$100 million equivalent). The initial IDA Financial Sector Stability Credit approved in June 2013, was a stand-alone single tranche credit in the amount of USD 30 million equivalent). The second and third credits (each in the amount of USD 100 million equivalent, and approved in June 2015 and March 2017, respectively), were designed in a programmatic series of three operations. The series has four pillars: (a) enhancing financial sector development; (b) restructuring and consolidating the financial system; (c) strengthening the legal and regulatory framework; and (d) enhancing the governance and transparency of the banking system.The proposed operation is consistent with the Country Partnership Strategy (CPS) for FY2014–2017 that acknowledges the persistent financial sector weakness and the risk it poses to macroeconomic stability and economic growth. The Performance and Learning Review (PLR, FY2017) of the CPS also acknowledges the progress made through the series of DPCs, particularly in addressing the capital adequacy of state-owned banks, strengthening inspection and compliance, ensuring overall financial sector stability and contributing to access to finance. The Systematic Country Diagnostic (FY2018) highlights financial sector stability and inclusion as important aspects for broader economic growth and poverty reduction. The operation was prepared in close collaboration with the International Finance Corporation (IFC), the International Monetary Fund (IMF), and the United Kingdom Department for International Development (DFID).

title.narrative: Resolution powers of cooperative regulator and conversion of financial intermediary NGOs to licensed MFIs

baseline.value: (a) The NRB supervises only 15 financial cooperatives out of 17,000 operating. The remainder are licensed by the Registrar of Cooperatives, which has no supervisory authority and no resolution powers, and (b) there are 47 Financial Intermediary NGOs licensed by the NRB.

target.value: All NRB-authorized FINGOs MFIs have been converted to Class D microfinance banks.

actual.value: All NRB-authorized FINGOs MFIs have been converted to Class D microfinance banks. The new Cooperatives Act provides supervisory and resolution powers to the Registrar of Cooperatives.

title.narrative: Banking system stability is evidenced by all banks either being compliant with the CAR or being in NRB-approved PCA or resolution programs

baseline.value: Compliance-based supervision is inadequate to identify potential risks. Reported CAR is 12.03 percent for commercial banks, 15.6 percent for Class B, and 15.9 percent for Class C institutions. Under-capitalized banks not under PCA.

target.value: Banking system stability is evidenced by all banks either being compliant with the CAR or being in NRB-approved PCA or resolution programs.

actual.value: All the commercial banks meet the minimum CAR of 10 percent, with an industry average of 13.9 percent as of M8 FY2020. This includes 13.7 percent for commercial banks, 15.3 percent for Class B (development banks) and 19.4 percent for Class C (finance companies) institutions.

title.narrative: Financial Action Task Force (FATF) Grey List

baseline.value: Nepal is not on the FATF grey list.

target.value: Nepal remains off the FATF grey list which allows normal external financial relations (trade finance, remittance inflows and foreign direct investment).

actual.value: Nepal remains off the FATF grey list.

title.narrative: A strengthened coordination framework for design and implementation of financial sector reforms

baseline.value: No national FSDS is in place to guide policy and regulatory development

target.value: A strengthened coordination framework for design and implementation of financial sector reforms is established.

actual.value: The Cabinet approved the FSDS in January 2017. A High-level Financial Sector Coordination Committee has been set up to monitor progress and meets regularly. For the effective monitoring of the FSDS recommendations, two high-level committees were formed – one under the Chairmanship of the NRB Governor and the other under the Chairmanship of the Finance Minister

title.narrative: Minimization of operational risk with disaster recovery site and business continuity plan

baseline.value: Operational risk is high as the NRB does not have a Disaster Risk Site and the Business Continuity framework is inadequate.

target.value: Business Continuity framework and Disaster Risk Site established.

actual.value: Business Continuity framework for NRB and all commercial banks are in place and Disaster Risk Site established.

title.narrative: Adoption of Nepal Financial Reporting Standard (NFRS)

baseline.value: The NFRS has been implemented by 0 percent of Class A and Class B BFIs. NFRS-compliant regulations have not been issued by the NRB.

target.value: NFRS has been implemented by 100 percent of Class A and Class B BFIs.

actual.value: NFRS has been implemented by all Class A and Class B BFIs as of Q1 (mid-October) of FY 2019/20.

title.narrative: Strengthened supervisory capacity of NRB, compliance with four more BCPs and implementation of a new supervisory information system

baseline.value: The NRB is non-compliant or materially non-compliant with many BCPs and lacks an adequate IT system to support supervision. Financial reporting by FIs involves manual processing and results in errors.

target.value: The NRB has strengthened its supervisory capacity and is largely compliant with four more Basel Core Principle (BCPs) and a new SIShas been implemented.

actual.value: (i) The SIS was successfully launched in October 2019 with all commercial banks are connected on real-time basis from December 2019. (ii) As per strategic program for FY 2019/20, NRB has announced observance of additional BCPs for effective bank supervision practices. Accordingly, the NRB focused on banks internal control system (BCP # 14), prevention of fraud and money-laundering (#15), overall framework for on-site and off-site supervision (#16) and maintaining increased contacts with bank management and staff (#17). Self-assessment conducted with the support of IMF Resident Advisor in the observance of these BCPs have been assessed as ‘largely compliant’.

title.narrative: The RBB meets all regulatory norms, the bank has positive net income and Board of Directors meet professional qualification

baseline.value: The RBB is 100 percent state owned and undercapitalized (July 2014 CAR=5.60 percent).

target.value: The RBB's CAR is above 11 percent, Positive Net Income for preceding four quarters, and composition of RBB Board complies with NRB directive.

actual.value: The RBB's CAR stands at 13.15 percent as of Q2 FY2020 and the bank registered positive net income for last four quarters, totaling NPR 5.1 billion. The board of directors meets the required professional qualifications

title.narrative: Reduction in the number of BFIs

baseline.value: The banking system is characterized by an excessive number of FIs (January 2012=199, July 2014=167). Banking regulations impede theuse of acquisitions as a means of consolidation

target.value: The total number of BFIs is reduced to 130 or less.

actual.value: The total number of BFIs stands at 72 as of M8 FY 2020.

title.narrative: DCGF as Administrator of Deposit Guarantee Fund and all BFIs current in payment of premiums

baseline.value: The deposit insurance system has a very weak legal framework based on DCGC bylaws. The DCGC lacks any IT system to administer the system and the regulatory framework for deposit insurance is largely incomplete.

target.value: Legal framework is in place for the DCGF to be the administrator of the DGF. All BFIs have made required deposit guarantee premium payments for the preceding four quarters.

actual.value: The legal framework is in place and all BFIs have made required deposit guarantee premium payments for the preceding four quarters.The paid-up capital of DCGF was increased to NPR 10 billion as of Q4FY 2019.

title.narrative: Legal and institutional framework for financial crisis management

baseline.value: The financial crisis management architecture is limited to a High-Level Financial Sector Committee with the power to coordinate government responses but without special anti-crisis intervention powers, and emergency liquidity assistance is inadequate.

target.value: The framework for contingency back-up funding for bank resolution is established.

actual.value: The framework for back-up funding is established.

title.narrative: The NBL meets all regulatory norms, has positive net income and has decreased government ownership

baseline.value: The government controls two large commercial banks. The NBL is undercapitalized (July 2014 CAR=5.26 percent) and majority owned (63percent) by the government.

target.value: The NBL meets all regulatory norms (including CAR > 10 percent), has positive net income for the preceding four quarters, and has decreased government ownership.

actual.value: The NBL's CAR is 17.4 percent as of Q2 FY2020, and the bank registered positive net income for last four quarters, totaling NPR 2.3billion. Divestment of government to 51 percent. The board of directors meets the required professional qualifications.

title.narrative: A modernized legal framework for bank resolution and implementing regulations

baseline.value: The legal framework for bank resolution is outdated and incomplete, limiting the NRB's ability to resolve FIs quickly. Conflicts between laws provide scope for FIs to challenge the NRB's resolution authority. The NRB's Prompt & Corrective (PCA) framework reflectsthe limited resolution powers given to the NRB under existing laws.

target.value: A modernized legal framework for bank resolution is in place and implementing regulations have been issued by the NRB.

actual.value: The bill was approved by the Parliament in September 2016. The implementing regulations (including amendments to existing regulations) have been issued through various circulars and directives.

title.narrative: Framework to regulate/supervise payments system institutions and elimination of settlement risk

baseline.value: The payments system regulation lacks a firm legal foundation and is subject to patchwork supervision by different regulators. Financial institutions face settlement risk owing to a lack of coordinated operations between NRB and other payments system institution. Quality of large value payment system is assessed as “low”.

target.value: Safety and efficiency of payment and settlement systems improved as evidenced by the quality of the large value payments being assessed as “medium-high”.

actual.value: Following the enactment of Payment and Settlement Act in March 2019, all bank and non-bank institutions involved in payment transactions are governed by regulatory framework of the NRB. The quality has been revised upwards from “medium-low” to “medium-high” upon operationalization of Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) on November 22, 2019.

title.narrative: Compliance with Fit and Proper Criteria in the appointment of CEO and Board of Directors of all BFIs

baseline.value: Under current law governance provisions are weak and give rise to numerous conflicts of interest on the part of bank directors who lack independence from shareholders. Professional qualifications requirements for directors and senior managers are limited and government-appointed CEOs and directors of two state-controlled commercial banks are exempt from qualifications requirements.

target.value: All board of directors, members and CEOs of banks and financial institutions, including state-controlled banks, meet the fit and proper criteria defined in the new BAFIA and NRB Directives.

actual.value: All board of directors members and CEOs of banks and FIs, including state-controlled banks, meet the fit and proper criteria defined in the new BAFIA and NRB directives.

title.narrative: Compliance by insurance companies with minimum capital and technical reserve requirements or under corrective action or resolution program of NIB

baseline.value: The NIB lacks adequate and accurate financial and risk information to identify troubled insurance companies and assess the impact of earthquake losses on their technical reserves and capital.

target.value: All insurance companies are adequately capitalized (new requirement of NPR 2 billion for life and NPR 1 billion for non-life to be met by FYE 2018) or are subject to corrective action/resolution program.

actual.value: The insurance companies have implemented NFRS as of Q1 2019/20 (mid-October 2019). Data of FY end 2019 from NIB shows three (two ofwhich are state-controlled) of the 39 insurance companies did not meeting minimum capital requirement. The state-controlled companies have been directed to meet capital requirement. The private company (Gurans Life), which did not meet requirement, have started the process of issuing 1:1 rights share to raise capital.

title.narrative: Modern legal and regulatory framework empowering Nepal Insurance Board to resolve troubled insurance companies

baseline.value: The Insurance Act is outdated and does not give the Insurance Board adequate powers to regulate and supervise the sector. The Insurance Board's ability to resolve under-capitalized insurance companies is limited.

target.value: The legal framework for supervision and regulation of the insurance sector has been modernized and the NIB is able to intervene effectively to resolve troubled insurance companies.

actual.value: (i) The Bill is currently with the Parliament for approval; (ii) NIB is able to intervene effectively to resolve troubled insurancecompanies under regulatory framework.

title.narrative: Resolution framework to deal with problematic co-operatives and compliance of new gender requirement

baseline.value: There is no resolution framework to address problematic financial cooperatives. Women are under-represented in the governance structure of the co-operatives.

target.value: Resolution framework is in place to deal with problematic co-operatives and 90 percent of the co-operatives have met the new genderrequirement.

actual.value: (i) The provision for dealing with problematic co-operatives is in place as per Cooperatives Act; and (ii) Women representation in the board of directors is 40.1 percent from data of 13,578 registered Savings and & Credit Cooperatives (Source: Cooperatives Statistics 2018). However, data is not available to determine if each of the cooperatives have one-third board members as women.
